documents: Jordan et al. 2022, JGR Earth Surface 127, e2022JF006673 (published paper, PDF, 24 pp.)

entry.evidence: it is often unclear how ice fabric and its spatial variability impact on ice flow and stability across the ice sheets

steps.action: Pose the question of how ice fabric and its spatial variability affect ice viscosity and flow in fast-flowing ice streams, where measurements are scarce.
steps.quote: it is often unclear how ice fabric and its spatial variability impact on ice flow and stability across the ice sheets

steps.action: Take from prior work the claims that fabric softens Rutford Ice Stream margins to lateral shear (Minchew et al. 2018) and that a horizontal partial girdle exists (Smith et al. 2017).
steps.quote: Minchew et al. (2018) inferred that the ice fabric has a softening effect on lateral shear within the margins of Rutford Ice Stream

steps.action: Acquire quad-polarized ApRES radar soundings at 20 sites on two transects, one across flow from centre to margin (2017) and one along the central flow line (2019).
steps.quote: The ground-based radar survey consists of 20 discrete measurement sites along two separate transects.

steps.action: Derive the ice-surface strain-rate tensor, in principal and flow coordinates, from MEaSUREs velocities with a Gaussian convolution derivative, with a Monte Carlo ensemble for uncertainty (results in Section 6.1, Figure 6).
steps.quote: D was initially computed in polar stereographic coordinates by differentiating horizontal ice-surface velocity components from the MEaSUREs data product

steps.action: Represent fabric by the second-order orientation tensor, bound all three eigenvalues from the radar-measured horizontal eigenvalue difference under three principal-axis orientation models (Figure 2), and set up the polarimetric coherence method.
steps.quote: we consider three model permutations of the principal axis relative to the ice-sheet coordinates

steps.action: Validate the rotation basis transformation by checking conserved quantities, and test sensitivity to the 40 m coherence window (supplement).
steps.quote: validated by checking for conserved quantities

steps.action: Develop automated extraction of fabric orientation, using a symmetry-constraint cost function, and of fabric strength, with antenna-alignment and decoherence uncertainty propagated.
steps.quote: we describe new method development that improves automation of the fabric estimates from previous studies

steps.action: Test the retrieval on synthetic depth profiles for three cases (depth-invariant, sharp 90° rotation, gradual rotation), showing agreement for cases 1-2 and bias for case 3.
steps.quote: The examples in Figures 4a and 4b illustrate agreement between the true (synthetic) and retrieved (fitted) values

steps.action: Build a framework that feeds radar fabric bounds into the GOLF orthotropic flow law (ElmerIce AIFlow) to bound effective viscosity tensor elements, and map these for general fabric states (Figure 5).
steps.quote: The new contribution here is to consider how the azimuthal cross section of the fabric that is measured by the radar

steps.action: Estimate fabric orientation and strength profiles at each site and define depth units U1 (40-80 m) and U2 (120-160 m) for comparison between sites.
steps.quote: The azimuthal fabric strength generally increases toward the ice-stream margin

steps.action: Establish that the upstream sites B8-B10 consistently show two subunits with a ~90° azimuthal fabric rotation near 100 m depth.
steps.quote: These three sites all approximate the backscatter simulations for a 90° azimuthal rotation in ice fabric within the ice column

steps.action: State the hypothesis that near-surface fabric reflects strain-induced development matching the local ice flow.
steps.quote: The comparison is made to test the hypothesis that the fabric nearer the ice surface is consistent with strain-induced development

steps.action: Compare U1 fabric orientation and strength with the compression angle and magnitude along Transect A: close correlation with a ~-10° offset.
steps.quote: The fabric orientation is closely correlated with the compression angle, rotating counterclockwise by approximately 55° between sites A1 and A9

steps.action: Repeat the comparison on the independent along-flow Transect B: U1 agrees with compression direction at both ends but correlates less well where strain is weak, while U2 is aligned along flow throughout.
steps.quote: at the downstream site B2, the fabric and compression axes are both orientated along-flow

steps.action: Bound effective viscosities (tttt, nnnn, tntn) along Transects A and B, finding local hardening to lateral shear toward the margin and a depth transition in uniaxial viscosities at B8-B10.
steps.quote: all three orientation models predict that ice locally hardens to lateral shear

steps.action: Show the viscosity range for all three orientation models and propagate fabric measurement uncertainty by ensemble, giving less than 5% fractional uncertainty.
steps.quote: we also propagated the measurement uncertainties of fabric strength and orientation using an ensemble approach

steps.action: Take from theory and experiments the prediction of alignment with compression for flow-induced fabric, with deviation up to 45° under simple shear.
steps.quote: deviations from the simple relationship between compression and c-axis alignment are predicted for ice undergoing simple shear

steps.action: Compare margin observations with the simple-shear prediction: the deviation from compression alignment is small.
steps.quote: the predicted deviation from alignment with compression due to rigid body rotation (Azuma & Higashi, 1985; Fujita & Mae, 1994) is relatively small

steps.action: Explain the discrepancy by revising the finite-strain auxiliary (shallow fabric is transient and still developing), supported by Llorens et al. (2016), rather than rejecting flow-induced development.
steps.quote: An explanation for this discrepancy is that the shallow-ice fabric in U1 is in a transient state and still developing with ice depth.

steps.action: Pose rival explanations for U2 misalignment: upstream-formed fabric advected and buried, versus temporal changes in the surface strain field.
steps.quote: Alternatively, temporal changes in the surface strain field could contribute to the observed difference between the surface strain and unit U2.

steps.action: Compare U2 orientation with the strain field 20-30 km upstream, where along-flow compression supports the advection explanation; temporal change is not excluded.
steps.quote: This assertion is supported by the presence of along-flow compression in the surface ice ≈20–30 km upstream of site B10

steps.action: Set the inferred margin hardening to lateral shear against the model-based softening inferred by Minchew et al. (2018).
steps.quote: This finding differs from Minchew et al. (2018) who, via a model-based approach, inferred that the fabric has a softening effect

steps.action: Reconcile the two results by restricting the shallow-ice result: shear-softening fabric may be present in deeper ice.
steps.quote: fabric and viscosity of the shallow-ice layer near the shear margin are likely to be unrepresentative of the majority of the ice column

steps.action: Compare radar fabric with seismic shear-wave splitting (Smith et al. 2017): both show azimuthal anisotropy but with differing orientations; the deep high-coherence band supports a vertical cluster.
steps.quote: Both radar and seismic data sets indicate azimuthal anisotropy although there are differing orientations for the direction of greatest horizontal c-axis alignment.

steps.action: Attribute the discrepancy to seismic depth-averaging and limit the U2 result to thin near-surface layers.
steps.quote: it is unlikely that unit U2 is representative of the rest of the ice column

steps.action: Keep the conclusions: shallow fabric is aligned with surface compression; deeper fabric is rotated and inherited from upstream; spatial fabric variation gives bounded lateral and depth variation in anisotropic viscosity.
steps.quote: Spatial variation in ice fabric translates to lateral and depth variations in the anisotropic viscosity of ice.

end.claim: Radar-inferred fabric in the top 40-300 m of Rutford Ice Stream varies sharply laterally and with depth (aligned with surface compression in shallow ice, rotated up to ~90° deeper), and this translates into bounded lateral and depth variations in anisotropic viscosity that isotropic flow models cannot represent.

decisive_move.sentence: The framework that converts radar-measured azimuthal fabric bounds into bounds on GOLF effective viscosity tensor elements is what makes the viscosity claims possible.

gates.evidence: The surveys (2017, 2019, BEAMISH project) are not described as directed by a stated hypothesis. The alignment hypothesis (p. 15) is tested against the observed strain field and could have failed; it partly did in U2 and at weak-strain sites. The viscosity bounds are estimates, not tested against an independent outcome. Nothing is reported as fixed in advance; the depth units and the coherence filter threshold were set while analysing the data (p. 12-14).

imports.field: radar remote sensing / SAR interferometry and polarimetry
imports.item: polarimetric coherence phase as an analogue of interferometric phase; scattering-matrix rotation and conserved quantities (Boerner 1992)
Cramer-Rao bound for phase error from coherence magnitude (Touzi & Lopes 1999)
linear orthotropic flow law with a viscoplastic self-consistent polycrystal model (GOLF; Castelnau et al. 1996)

novelty_claims.quote: have not been used to constrain anisotropic viscosity. To address this deficiency, we develop a new framework
we describe new method development that improves automation of the fabric estimates from previous studies
The new contribution here is to consider how the azimuthal cross section of the fabric that is measured by the radar
represents a new challenge for models that invert for basal conditions and viscosity from surface strain-rates

limits: No peer-review file was supplied; only the acknowledgment of two anonymous reviewers is known, so question 9 is uncoded. Sub-claim statuses: (a) alignment of shallow fabric with surface compression is confirmed in a weak sense: tested against strain, but with no explicit rival to flow-induced development; (b) upstream fabric advected and preserved at depth is best_explanation, since temporal strain change is not excluded (p. 20); (c) the radar-to-viscosity framework is capability_characterized, tested on synthetic data for fabric retrieval only, not for viscosity; (d) shallow margin ice shows no shear softening, a regularity limited to the top ~100 m. The vertical fabric component is unknown, so viscosity is only bounded across three orientation models; the preferred x3/x2 vertical models rest on cited modelling (Lilien et al. 2021). Inference by the coder: the choice of composition (capability_first) reflects a method-led walk with a hypothesis test embedded; trace_series would also be defensible for the discussion of advection. The paper does not report how the U1/U2 depth bounds, the |c|>0.5 filter, or the permittivity values were chosen against alternatives, nor whether analysis choices were revised after seeing the data. The window-size sensitivity is only referenced to the supplement, which was not supplied.

disagreements.support: Radar-bounded viscosities show near-surface hardening to lateral shear at A6-A9 under all three orientation models; the authors reconcile this by proposing that softening fabric lies in deeper ice.
disagreements.quote: This finding differs from Minchew et al. (2018) who, via a model-based approach, inferred that the fabric has a softening effect

disagreements.target: Smith et al. (2017) seismic shear-wave splitting fabric
disagreements.support: U2 fabric is along-flow while the seismic bulk fabric is perpendicular to flow; the authors attribute this to seismic depth-averaging and treat U2 as unrepresentative of the full column.
disagreements.quote: in the seismic interpretation of the full ice column by Smith et al. (2017), the fabric of the bulk ice column is perpendicular to flow

disagreements.target: Predicted rigid-body-rotation deviation under simple shear (Azuma & Higashi 1985; Fujita & Mae 1994)
disagreements.support: Near the margin, the observed fabric deviates only slightly from the compression axis, which the authors explain as a transient early-stage fabric.
disagreements.quote: the predicted deviation from alignment with compression due to rigid body rotation (Azuma & Higashi, 1985; Fujita & Mae, 1994) is relatively small

disagreements.target: Previous radar-sounding studies assuming x3 vertical
disagreements.support: The authors consider all three principal-axis orientation models as end-members, citing evidence that x1 or x2 may be vertical near shear margins.
disagreements.quote: Previous radar-sounding studies have assumed that the x3 axis (direction of greatest c-axis alignment) is vertical

disagreements.target: Isotropic inverse ice-sheet models (Goldberg 2011; Hindmarsh 2004; MacAyeal 1992; Schoof & Hindmarsh 2010)
disagreements.support: The depth transition in anisotropic viscosity at B8-B10 implies that isotropic inversions from surface strain miss depth-varying viscosity.
disagreements.quote: isotropic models generally do not account for that when deriving basal conditions
